topics.title: Teach the pattern, then test the design
topics.summary: A student should finish a lesson able to identify the problem that needs a pattern, point to each role in code and UML, trace how those roles work together, and explain when the pattern is unnecessary. Recognizing a class diagram by its shape is not enough. The design must solve a stated problem.

blocks.text: Start each chapter with its concrete problem and the simplest reasonable approach. Let the limitation become visible before introducing the new arrangement. Then name the pattern and connect its roles to the program. The role table maps the standard role, the attached sample's name, and the name used in this chapter. This is the bridge between the supplied reading and the original teaching example.

Use the attached-example trace to revisit the provided code. Follow calls or ownership changes in their actual order. Then compare the new program. Ask which relationships stay the same and which language or application choices changed. The section on adaptations distinguishes the pattern's essential mechanism from optional features of one sample.

For a classroom demonstration, show the problem first, sketch the roles next, predict the call sequence, and run the complete example. Pause at each focused diagram page. Its code, line reading, and adjacent theory explain one important block. Finish by changing a requirement and asking whether the same design still fits. Each chapter supplies a specific teaching sequence and pattern questions.

Use the independent exercises in order: make a guided change, trace unfamiliar behavior, diagnose a defect, compare designs, extend while keeping earlier checks, and justify a decision. The implementation lab is a larger change with a runnable starting point and an explained solution. Pattern-check answers and exercise answers are kept in the separate answer section.

Read the short primer before the first pattern if objects, interfaces, ownership, or SOLID are unfamiliar. It defines the language needed for the pattern lessons. The course itself begins with Factory Method and continues through all 22 named patterns. The capstone then asks students to select and combine techniques rather than force every pattern into one program.

topics.title: Build the demonstrations and read the diagrams
topics.summary: Extract the companion ZIP and run the commands below from its top-level directory. Each examples/chNN/main.cpp is a complete independent program. Its expected.txt file contains exactly what it should print. The program also checks its own behavior. The exercises and solutions directories contain the corresponding lab versions.

blocks.text: The -std=c++17 option selects the language version. The warning options ask the compiler to flag suspicious code, and -Werror makes those warnings stop the build. The -pthread option supports standard-library threading used by the Singleton lesson. The -o option names the executable. Python 3.9 or later runs the test driver without extra Python packages.

A class diagram shows types and their relationships. A hollow triangle points from a derived class to its base interface. A filled diamond sits at the exclusive owner. A hollow diamond labeled shared ownership marks shared ownership; the last strong owner controls release. A dashed dependency arrow means uses or borrows, not owns. Each diagram has a numbered relationship key.

Activity diagrams follow actions and decisions. Sequence diagrams read from top to bottom as calls occur. State diagrams show states and permitted changes between them. The diagram type is chosen to explain the lesson's central mechanism. Pattern roles are named alongside the actual types or participants where appropriate.

The blue dotted connector on a focused page is a teaching annotation. It links the exact C++ excerpt to the adjacent theory panel; it is not a UML relationship. The line-by-line reading explains every selected nonblank source line. Paths and inclusive line ranges match the delivered files and are recalculated when the book is rebuilt.

A passing program supports the cases it actually checks. The release verifies the new teaching code, not every platform, every possible execution, or every supplied archive variant. Source-sample limitations are discussed where they affect understanding. Full verification details and untested conditions are recorded in the rebuild kit.

blocks.code:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread \
  examples/ch01/main.cpp -o build/factory_method
./build/factory_method

topics.title: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern
topics.summary: This book teaches the patterns in the supplied reading and C++ examples. Its central question is "What change is hard, and which design makes it safer?" A design pattern is a named way to arrange program parts to solve a recurring problem. Its name helps a team discuss the problem, roles, and tradeoffs.

blocks.text: An algorithm is a set of steps that computes a result, such as finding the largest number. A pattern describes how responsibilities fit together, such as letting a caller choose among several algorithms. A library supplies usable code. A pattern supplies an idea that you must adapt. Two programs may use Strategy even though their class names, data, and algorithms differ.

Begin with a concrete requirement. A monitor must report one estimate from a list of readings. If the only rule is an average, one small function is enough. Now users need the highest reading too, and must switch rules during a run. A growing branch in the monitor mixes input checks with each rule. Strategy becomes useful when we want those rules to change independently. The extra objects have a cost, so two stable branches may still be the better choice.

Each chapter states a requirement, exposes the limit of a simple design, introduces the named pattern, traces and tests the solution, and judges an alternative. A pattern succeeds when it makes a real change easier while preserving required behavior. More classes or a familiar diagram do not prove better design.

topics.title: The object words used by the patterns
topics.summary: A type tells C++ what kind of value something holds and which operations are allowed. A class defines a type that can hold data and provide functions. An object is a particular instance with its own identity and lifetime. Two monitor objects can use the same class while holding different rules. A member is a variable or function declared in a class; a member function is also called a method.

blocks.text: An interface is the set of operations a caller can use, together with their promises. It is more than a list of function names. For an estimate, the promise might require a nonempty list and return a value inside a stated range. An abstraction keeps the facts a caller needs and leaves out details it does not need. The monitor needs "estimate these readings," not the exact steps for finding an average.

Encapsulation puts related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. Private members stop ordinary outside code from changing them directly. A monitor can reject a missing rule before replacing its current rule. Its invariant, a rule that must remain true at its public boundary, is that it has a usable rule. Merely making a field private does not protect it if a public operation still allows a bad value.

Inheritance defines one class in terms of a base class. Public inheritance says that a derived object can be used through the base type. This is a promise about behavior, not just a way to reuse lines. Polymorphism lets the same interface call reach different implementations. Through an Estimate reference, value() can run the Average or Highest implementation. C++ also supports other forms of polymorphism; these chapters mainly use virtual member functions.

Composition builds behavior by connecting objects. A monitor has a rule instead of inheriting every possible rule. In UML, strict composition also shows a strong whole-part lifetime relationship: the whole is responsible for its parts. In broader design advice, "favor composition" includes collaboration with borrowed objects too. Ownership means responsibility for an object or resource and its eventual release; access alone does not imply ownership.

A dependency means that changing one part can force another part to change. Passing a report type to a function creates a dependency on that type. An association is a lasting link between objects, such as a controller retaining access to a screen. Aggregation describes a whole-part grouping whose parts may live independently, such as a view grouping existing sensors. Its hollow diamond does not specify who deletes a C++ object. State ownership separately and check the actual code.

topics.title: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose
topics.summary: Good design makes required behavior clear and likely changes manageable. Cohesion means keeping closely related work together. Coupling means how strongly one part relies on another. A useful design often raises cohesion and limits unnecessary coupling. There is no useful rule that all coupling must disappear: cooperating parts must agree on something. Aim for a small, stable agreement that a reader can explain and a test can check.

blocks.text: Encapsulate what varies. If new output styles keep changing a report calculation, separate formatting from calculation. The stable calculation can produce a result while a formatter chooses its presentation. First identify evidence of change: repeated edits, duplicated branches, or different user needs. Do not build a framework for a variation nobody needs. A function parameter may isolate the variation before a family of classes is worth its cost.

Program to an interface. A job that needs to store a result should ask for the storage behavior it needs, rather than reach into one particular file writer. The caller depends on a promise; implementations fulfill that promise. This permits a test implementation that keeps results in memory. It does not mean every class needs a separate interface. If there is one small, stable implementation, calling it directly can be clearer.

Favor composition over inheritance when separate choices must vary independently. With two report types and three delivery methods, making a subclass for every pair leads to six combinations. Connecting a report object to a delivery object keeps the choices separate. Inheritance still fits a true substitution relationship and a stable shared workflow. The question is which arrangement matches the change, not which language feature sounds more advanced.

topics.title: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design
topics.summary: Single Responsibility Principle: keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module is a part of a program that we can discuss as a unit, often a class or file. Suppose one class both decides which readings count as alerts and writes a color report. New alert policy and new report styling come from different needs. Separating those jobs lets each change without disturbing the other. This principle does not mean one function per class or one method per object.

blocks.text: Open/Closed Principle: allow a planned kind of extension without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. Suppose the monitor validates readings and then asks an Estimate for a result. Adding a Median implementation can preserve that monitor code. The program still needs code or configuration that selects Median. "Closed" does not mean never fixing a bug or never changing a requirement. It means protecting a useful boundary from a known direction of change. A small fixed set of choices may need no extension boundary.

Liskov Substitution Principle: a derived type must keep the promises callers rely on from its base type. If Estimate accepts every nonempty list of values from 0 through 1000, an implementation that secretly requires at least ten values breaks that promise. It has strengthened a precondition, a condition required before a call. Returning a value outside a promised range weakens a postcondition, a guarantee after the call. Derived types must also preserve the base invariants. Test every implementation against the same contract, including small and boundary inputs.

Liskov substitution concerns behavior as well as legal C++ syntax. A method can compile with override and still return the wrong units or reject a valid request. Replacing a base parameter type with a different type normally does not override the function in C++; matching the required signature matters. Do not confuse the broad idea of accepting more cases with permission to change a C++ override signature. The compiler checks part of the contract; tests and review check the rest.

Interface Segregation Principle: a caller should not have to depend on operations it does not use. Suppose a small archive reader needs only load(), but its interface also requires save(), erase(), and network setup. A read-only implementation then needs fake operations or surprising failures. Split the meaningful capabilities so a reader depends on reading. One implementation may support several capabilities. Do not split every method into its own interface: the goal is a useful contract for each caller, not the largest possible number of types.

Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level policy and low-level detail should depend on suitable abstractions; the abstraction should not depend on the detail. High-level policy is the rule that says what the program must achieve. Low-level detail is how a device, file, or service carries it out. Let an alert policy depend on an AlertSink promise. A file sink and a test sink implement that promise. Changing the file format then need not change the alert decision.

Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside, often through a constructor. It can help implement dependency inversion, but the ideas are different. Passing a concrete file writer into a constructor is injection; policy can still depend directly on that writer. For inversion, inspect the types and their promises. SOLID principles help you ask questions. They are not five gates that force every small program to grow more classes.

topics.title: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles
topics.summary: The next excerpt becomes useful when an archive job must format records in different ways while keeping one workflow. Record names the common promise. TextRecord and BracketRecord provide choices in Chapter 1. A class body is inside braces, and the final semicolon ends the class declaration. public: marks members that callers may use. C++ has no separate interface keyword; an abstract class can express an interface.

blocks.text: Line by line: class Record begins the type. public: opens its public part. virtual ~Record() = default declares a virtual destructor and asks the compiler to supply its normal implementation. A destructor performs cleanup when an object is destroyed; the tilde marks its name. Virtual destruction makes deleting a derived record through the base pointer used by its owner safe. The format declaration returns a std::string, the standard library text type, and receives text as its input. The closing brace and semicolon finish the type.

In const std::string& text, the ampersand declares a reference: another name for an existing string, rather than a new string copy. const prevents changing that string through this reference. It does not promise that no other alias can change the same object. A value parameter would instead hold its own parameter object. The const after format(...) limits ordinary changes to the receiving object through that call. These two uses of const apply to different things.

virtual enables selection of an implementation through a base pointer or reference at run time. The = 0 marks a pure virtual function: this class leaves the operation to a derived implementation and cannot itself be instantiated. In a derived class, override asks the compiler to check that a function really overrides a base virtual function. final can prevent further derivation or overriding. Neither word proves the behavior is correct.

In Record* p, the star declares a pointer that holds an address and may be null. In *p, it follows the pointer to the object; a bad pointer makes that unsafe. p->format(text) calls a member through a pointer; a direct object uses a dot. A raw pointer does not state ownership. std::unique_ptr<Record> is an owning handle whose destructor releases its object. It permits one owner and cannot be copied. std::make_unique<TextRecord>() creates an object and returns its owner.

std::move(x) allows a move operation to be chosen; it does not itself move any object. Moving a unique_ptr into another owner transfers its object and leaves that particular source pointer empty. Do not assume all moved-from library objects are empty. The angle brackets in std::vector<int> or std::unique_ptr<Record> supply types to a library template, a reusable type recipe. You need to read these uses before you need to write templates.

In for (const auto& child : children), the colon means "take each element from children." auto asks the compiler to infer the element type; & borrows each element; const prevents changing that element through child. For a const unique_ptr this does not make the pointed-to object const. In a constructor, : member(value) instead starts member initialization. Context decides what the colon means. #include brings declarations from a header, std:: names the standard namespace, return supplies a result, and // starts a comment to the end of the line.

topics.title: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime
topics.summary: A UML class diagram shows types and their relationships. A solid line ending in a hollow triangle points from a derived class toward its base. A dashed line with an ordinary arrow shows a dependency. An association uses a solid line; an arrow, when present, shows navigable access. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of composition; a hollow diamond marks aggregation. A realization of an interface may use a dashed line with a hollow triangle. Read each page legend because line styles carry different meanings.

blocks.text: An activity diagram follows actions and decisions. Its arrows show possible execution flow, not inheritance. A sequence diagram places participants across the page and calls downward through time. A state diagram shows states and permitted transitions caused by events. An ownership view names owners, borrowed links, and the events that end lifetimes. Teaching links connect notes to code blocks; they are labeled annotations and are not UML relationships.

Compilation checks source syntax and many type rules, then produces code that the linker combines into a program. Missing definitions may fail at link time. Execution creates objects, selects branches, calls functions, and destroys objects. override errors can be caught during compilation. Choosing a valid but wrong strategy is an execution problem. Virtual calls preserve the required behavior of selecting the final override; a compiler may optimize how it achieves that behavior.

Trace four paths separately. Data moves as arguments and results. Control moves through calls and returns. Ownership moves only when the code transfers responsibility. Lifetime begins with successful object construction and ends with destruction. A borrowed reference does not keep an object alive. A retained pointer can outlive its target unless the design prevents that. In each chapter, ask who creates each object, who may call it, who releases it, and which tests cover those promises.

topics.title: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change
topics.summary: The catalog follows the supplied material: five creational patterns, seven structural patterns, and ten behavioral patterns. Creational patterns organize object creation. Structural patterns organize how parts fit together. Behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. The table is a starting point, not an automatic selector. Several patterns can fit one program; compare their intent before comparing their box shapes.

blocks.text: For a class session, spend ten minutes on the simple design, ten on a new need that breaks it, fifteen tracing the solution and diagram, and fifteen making and testing one change. Use ten minutes to compare alternatives. Adjust the time to the class; require learners to predict behavior before running code.

Follow the exercises: guided change, code trace, bug repair, design choice, tested extension, and plain-English justification. In the capstone, name each pattern role in the source and state one invariant per boundary. Correct output is necessary; explain why the design stays correct under change.

options: Virtual calls always create new objects.
Every valid input must now be accepted.
The signature matches, but behavior still needs review and tests.

rationales: override says nothing about who owns an object.
Dispatch selects a function implementation; it does not imply allocation.

topics.title: Foundations recall
topics.summary: Review the words and decisions used across every pattern.

cards.question: What is a design pattern?
cards.answer: A named arrangement of responsibilities that solves a recurring design problem. Identify the actual change pressure before choosing it.

cards.question: How does a pattern differ from an algorithm?
cards.answer: An algorithm supplies computational steps. A pattern describes how responsibilities collaborate and vary.

cards.question: What is an invariant?
cards.answer: A rule that must remain true at a stated program boundary, including after permitted operations.

cards.question: What does ownership mean in C++?
cards.answer: Responsibility for an object or resource and its eventual release. Merely holding a pointer or reference does not establish ownership.

cards.question: What does override check?
cards.answer: It asks the compiler to verify that the declaration overrides a base virtual function. It does not prove all behavioral promises.

cards.question: What does const T& express?
cards.answer: A reference borrowing an existing T object, preventing mutation through that reference. Another alias may still change the object.

cards.question: When is a simpler design enough?
cards.answer: When direct functions, a small branch, or a value type meet the requirements without needing the variation boundary a pattern introduces.

cards.question: What must agree in a useful UML lesson?
cards.answer: The relationship legend, diagram blocks, source code, call trace, and lifetime rules must describe the same implementation.

workshop.title: Change a rule without copying the work
workshop.problem: A monitor must test the same reading against different limits. Start by making the changing value an input; a class hierarchy is not needed for this requirement.

steps.why: The comparison > asks whether 8 is greater than 10. bool holds true or false; the default stream prints false as 0.
The same operation uses a different input. No validation or call flow has been copied.

steps.state: A rolling-average policy would need more than a limit
steps.why: When the algorithm itself varies, Chapter 20 compares a policy interface with simpler function-based choices.

workshop.pitfall: Copying the whole monitor for every threshold spreads the same checks across several places. A bug fix can then reach one copy and miss another.

discussion.question: Should this two-threshold requirement use Strategy already?
discussion.answer: A function with a limit parameter is enough. Strategy becomes useful when whole algorithms vary behind a stable promise. Name the change before choosing a pattern; do not introduce a hierarchy just to change one integer.

workshop.alternative: A direct comparison is enough at one call site. A function is useful when the meaning is shared and deserves one named contract.
invariants: A value equal to the limit is not above it.
The function does not change the reading.
